God knows what is in man, and he knows what is in all creatures; he has therefore graciously forbidden what would injure both body and mind, and commanded what is best calculated to be useful to both. Solid-footed animals, such as the horse, and many-toed animals, such as the cat, etc., are here prohibited. Beasts which have bifid or cloven hoofs, such as the ox and sheep, are considered as proper for food, and therefore commanded. The former are unclean, i. e., unwholesome, affording a gross nutriment, often the parent of scorbutic and scrofulous disorders; the latter clean, i. e., affording a copious and wholesome nutriment, and not laying the foundation of any disease. Ruminating animals, i. e., those which chew the cud, concoct their food better than the others which swallow it with little mastication, and therefore their flesh contains more of the nutritious juices, and is more easy of digestion, and consequently of assimilation to the solids and fluids of the human body; on this account they are termed clean, i. e., peculiarly wholesome, and fit for food. The animals which do not ruminate do not concoct their food so well, and hence they abound with gross animal juices, which yield a comparatively unwholesome nutriment to the human system. Even the animals which have bifid hoofs but do not chew the cud, such as the swine, and those which chew the cud but are not bifid, such as the hare and rabbit, are by Him who knows all things forbidden, because he knew them to be comparatively innutritive. In all this God shows himself as the tender Father of a numerous family, pointing out to his inexperienced, froward, and ignorant children, those kinds of aliments which he knows will be injurious to their health and domestic happiness, and prohibiting them on pain of his highest displeasure. On the same ground he forbade all fish that have not both fins and scales, such as the conger, eel, etc., which abound in gross juices and fat which very few stomachs are able to digest. Who, for instance, that lives solely on swine's flesh, has pure blood and healthy juices? And is it not evident, in many cases, that the man partakes considerably of the nature of the brute on which he exclusively feeds? I could pursue this inquiry much farther, and bring many proofs founded on indisputable facts, but I forbear; for he who might stand most in need of caution, would be the first to take offense. <div eID="gen4647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4648" type="x-p"/> 3. As the body exists only for the sake of the soul, and God feeds and nourishes it through the day of probation, that the soul may here be prepared for the kingdom of heaven; therefore he shows in the conclusion of these ordinances, that the grand scope and design of all was that they might be a holy people, and that they might resemble him who is a holy God - God Is Holy; and this is the eternal reason why all his people should be holy - should be purified from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. No faith in any particular creed, no religious observance, no acts of benevolence and charity, no mortification, attrition, or contrition, can be a substitute for this. We must be made partakers of the Divine nature. We must be saved from our sins - from the corruption that is in the world, and be made holy within and righteous without, or never see God. For this very purpose Jesus Christ lived, died, and revived, that he might purify us unto himself; that through faith in his blood our sins might be blotted out, and our souls restored to the image of God - Reader, art thou hungering and thirsting after righteousness? Then blessed art thou, for thou shalt be filled.  <chapter eID="Lev.11"/> <div eID="gen4648" type="x-p"/>

entries.30e7bc3d29edf718f05acdea58ab02eb9d0ba816: <div eID="gen1278" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Laws Relating to Clean and Unclean Animals - Leviticus 11</title> <div sID="gen1279" type="x-p"/> The regulation of the sacrifices and institution of the priesthood, by which Jehovah opened up to His people the way of access to His grace and the way to sanctification of life in fellowship with Him, were followed by instructions concerning the various things which hindered and disturbed this living fellowship with God the Holy One, as being manifestations and results of sin, and by certain rules for avoiding and removing these obstructions. For example, although sin has its origin and proper seat in the soul, it pervades the whole body as the organ of the soul, and shatters the life of the body, even to its complete dissolution in death and decomposition; whilst its effects have spread from man to the whole of the earthly creation, inasmuch as not only did man draw nature with him into the service of sin, in consequence of the dominion over it which was given him by God, but God Himself, according to a holy law of His wise and equitable government, made the irrational creature subject to “vanity” and “corruption” on account of the sin of man (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.20-Rom.8.21">Rom 8:20-21</reference>), so that not only did the field bring forth thorns and thistles, and the earth produce injurious and poisonous plants (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Gen 3:18</reference>), but the animal kingdom in many of its forms and creatures bears the image of sin and death, and is constantly reminding man of the evil fruit of his fall from God. It is in this penetration of sin into the material creation that we may find the explanation of the fact, that from the very earliest times men have neither used every kind of herb nor every kind of animal as food; but that, whilst they have, as it were, instinctively avoided certain plants as injurious to health or destructive to life, they have also had a <hi type="italic">horror naturalis</hi>, i.e., an inexplicable disgust, at many of the animals, and have avoided their flesh as unclean. A similar horror must have been produced upon man from the very first, before his heart was altogether hardened, by death as the wages of sin, or rather by the effects of death, viz., the decomposition of the body; and different diseases and states of the body, that were connected with symptoms of corruption and decomposition, may also have been regarded as rendering unclean. Hence in all the nations and all the religions of antiquity we find that contrast between clean and unclean, which was developed in a dualistic form, it is true, in many of the religious systems, but had its primary root in the corruption that had entered the world through sin. This contrast was limited in the Mosaic law to the animal food of the Israelites, to contact with dead animals and human corpses, and to certain bodily conditions and diseases that are associated with the decomposition, pointing out most minutely the unclean objects and various defilements within these spheres, and prescribing the means for avoiding or removing them. <div eID="gen1279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1280" type="x-p"/> The instructions in the chapter before us, concerning the clean and unclean animals, are introduced in the first place as laws of food (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.2">Lev 11:2</reference>); but they pass beyond these bounds by prohibiting at the same time all contact with animal carrion (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.8">Lev 11:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.11">Lev 11:11</reference>, Lev 11:24.), and show thereby that they are connected in principle and object with the subsequent laws of purification (ch. 12-15), to which they are to be regarded as a preparatory introduction. <div eID="gen1280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1281" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lev.11.1">Lev 11:1</reference> <div eID="gen1281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1282" type="x-p"/> The laws which follow were given to Moses and Aaron (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.1">Lev 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.13.1">Lev 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.15.1">Lev 15:1</reference>), as Aaron had been sanctified through the anointing to expiate the sins and uncleannesses of the children of Israel.
entries.a80f3c99bf9e705e6dc206a1c43d5bc059254485: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.2-Lev.11.3">Lev 11:2-3</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.14.4-Deut.14.8">Deu 14:4-8</reference>). Of the larger quadrupeds, which are divided in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.24-Gen.1.25">Gen 1:24-25</reference> into beasts of the earth (living wild) and tame cattle, only the cattle (behemah) are mentioned here, as denoting the larger land animals, some of which were reared by man as domesticated animals, and others used as food. Of these the Israelites might eat “<hi type="italic">whatsoever parteth the hoof and is cloven-footed, and cheweth the cud among the cattle</hi>.” פּרסת שׁסע שׁסעת, literally “tearing (having) a rent in the hoofs,” according to <reference osisRef="Deut.14.5">Deu 14:5</reference> into “two claws,” i.e., with a hoof completely severed in two. גּרה, rumination, μηρυκισμός (lxx), from גּרר (cf. יגּר <reference osisRef="Lev.11.7">Lev 11:7</reference>), to draw (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.15">Hab 1:15</reference>), to draw to and fro; hence to bring up the food again, to ruminate. גּרה מעלת is connected with the preceding words with <hi type="italic">vav cop</hi>. to indicate the close connection of the two regulations, viz., that there was to be the perfectly cloven foot as well as the rumination (cf. Lev 11:4.). These marks are combined in the oxen, sheep, and goats, and also in the stag and gazelle. The latter are expressly mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.14.4-Deut.14.5">Deu 14:4-5</reference>, where - in addition to the <hi type="italic">common stag</hi> (איּל) and <hi type="italic">gazelle</hi> (צבי, δορκάς, lxx), or <hi type="italic">dorcas-antelope</hi>, which is most frequently met with in Palestine, Syria, and Arabia, of the size of a roebuck, with a reddish brown back and white body, horns sixteen inches long, and fine dark eyes, and the flesh of which, according to <hi type="italic">Avicenna</hi>, is the best of all the wild game-the following five are also selected, viz.: (1) יחמוּר, not βούβαλος, the buffalo (lxx, and <hi type="italic">Luther</hi>), but <hi type="italic">Damhirsch</hi>, a stag which is still much more common in Asia than in Europe and Palestine (see <hi type="italic">v. Schubert, </hi> R. iii. p. 118); (2) אקּו, probably, according to the Chaldee, <hi type="italic">Syriac</hi>, etc., the <hi type="italic">capricorn</hi> (<hi type="italic">Steinbock</hi>), which is very common in Palestine, not τραγέλαφος (lxx, Vulg.), the buck-stag (<hi type="italic">Bockhirsch</hi>), an animal lately discovered in Nubia (cf. <hi type="italic">Leyrer</hi> in <hi type="italic">Herzog's</hi> Cycl. vi. p. 143); (3) דּישׁן, according to the lxx and <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>. πύραργος, a kind of <hi type="italic">antelope</hi> resembling the stag, which is met with in Africa (Herod. 4, 192), - according to the Chaldee and Syriac, the <hi type="italic">buffalo-antelope</hi>, - according to the Samar. and Arabic, the <hi type="italic">mountain-stag;</hi> (4) תּאו, according to the Chaldee the <hi type="italic">wild ox,</hi> which is also met with in Egypt and Arabia, probably the oryx (lxx, Vulg.), a species of antelope as large as a stag; and (5) זמר, according to the lxx and most of the ancient versions, the <hi type="italic">giraffe</hi>, but this is only found in the deserts of Africa, and would hardly be met with even in Egypt-it is more probably <hi type="italic">capreae sylvestris species</hi>, according to the Chaldee.
entries.934aa0774d8281d5e5e200f0dab656b8dc9ea778: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.4-Lev.11.6">Lev 11:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen1282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1283" type="x-p"/> Any animal which was wanting in either of these marks was to be unclean, or not to be eaten. This is the case with the <hi type="italic">camel</hi>, whose flesh is eaten by the Arabs; it ruminates, but it has not cloven hoofs. Its foot is severed, it is true, but not thoroughly cloven, as there is a ball behind, upon which it treads. The <hi type="italic">hare</hi> and <hi type="italic">hyrax</hi> (<hi type="italic">Klippdachs</hi>) were also unclean, because, although they ruminate, they have not cloven hoofs. It is true that modern naturalists affirm that the two latter do not ruminate at all, as they have not the four stomachs that are common to ruminant animals; but they move the jaw sometimes in a manner which looks like ruminating, so that even <hi type="italic">Linnaeus</hi> affirmed that the hare chewed the cud, and Moses followed the popular opinion. According to <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>, <hi type="italic">Oedmann</hi>, and others, the <hi type="italic">shaphan</hi> is the <hi type="italic">jerboa</hi>, and according to the Rabbins and Luther, the rabbit or coney. But the more correct view is, that it is the <hi type="italic">wabr</hi> of the Arabs, which is still called <hi type="italic">tsofun</hi> in Southern Arabia (<hi type="italic">hyrax Syriacus</hi>), an animal which feeds on plants, a native of the countries of the Lebanon and Jordan, also of Arabia and Africa. They live in the natural caves and clefts of the rocks (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.18">Psa 104:18</reference>), are very gregarious, being often seen seated in troops before the openings to their caves, and extremely timid as they are quite defenceless (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.26">Pro 30:26</reference>). They are about the size of rabbits, of a brownish grey or brownish yellow colour, but white under the belly; they have bright eyes, round ears, and no tail. The Arabs eat them, but do not place them before their guests.<note placement="foot">See <hi type="italic">Shaw</hi>, iii. p. 301; Seetzen, ii. p. 228; Robinson<hi type="italic">'s</hi> <hi type="italic">Biblical Researches</hi>, p. 387; and Roediger on Gesenius <hi type="italic">thesaurus</hi>, p. 1467.</note>
entries.eb98523ddd5bf4897e132d4ca5aa8f3d0bab5d8e: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.7">Lev 11:7</reference> <div eID="gen1283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1284" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">swine</hi> has cloven hoofs, but does not ruminate; and many of the tribes of antiquity abstained from eating it, partly on account of its uncleanliness, and partly from fear of skin-diseases.
entries.2a05a2714ccd0e4f5701584575dbb90f0ee395f6: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.8">Lev 11:8</reference> <div eID="gen1284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1285" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Of their flesh shall ye not eat</hi> (i.e., not slay these animals as food), <hi type="italic">and their carcase</hi> (animals that had died) <hi type="italic">shall ye not touch</hi>.” The latter applied to the clean or edible animals also, when they had died a natural death (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.39">Lev 11:39</reference>).
entries.5d064194de0bf393ddd0f9713c316a0f5293191e: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.9-Lev.11.12">Lev 11:9-12</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.14.9">Deu 14:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.14.10">Deu 14:10</reference>). Of <hi type="italic">water animals</hi>, everything in the water, in seas and brooks, that had fins and scales was edible. Everything else that swarmed in the water was to be an abomination, its flesh was not to be eaten, and its carrion was to be avoided with abhorrence. Consequently, not only were all water animals other than fishes, such as crabs, salamanders, etc., forbidden as unclean; but also fishes without scales, such as eels for example. Numa laid down this law for the Romans: <hi type="italic">ut pisces qui sqamosi non essent ni pollicerent</hi> (sacrificed): <hi type="italic">Plin. h. n.</hi> 32, c. 2, s. 10. In Egypt fishes without scales are still regarded as unwholesome (<hi type="italic">Lane</hi>, Manners and Customs).
entries.43669fcf494b04ebcba0fa8e0b0e9d56b2348c84: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.13-Lev.11.14">Lev 11:13-14</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.14.11-Deut.14.18">Deu 14:11-18</reference>). Of <hi type="italic">birds</hi>, twenty varieties are prohibited, including the <hi type="italic">bat</hi>, but without any common mark being given; though they consist almost exclusively of birds which live upon flesh or carrion, and are most of them natives of Western Asia.<note placement="foot">The list is “hardly intended to be exhaustive, but simply mentions those which were eaten by others, and in relation to which, therefore, it was necessary that the Israelites should receive a special prohibition against eating them” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). Hence in Deuteronomy Moses added the ראה and enumerated twenty-one varieties; and on doubt, under other circumstances, he could have made the list still longer. In <reference osisRef="Deut.14.11">Deu 14:11</reference> צפּור is used, as synonymous with עוף in Deu 14:20.</note> <div eID="gen1285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1286" type="x-p"/> The list commences with the <hi type="italic">eagle</hi>, as the king of the birds. Nesher embraces all the species of eagles proper. The idea that the eagle will not touch carrion is erroneous. According to the testimony of Arabian writers (<hi type="italic">Damiri</hi> in <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>, ii. p. 577), and several naturalists who have travelled (e.g., <hi type="italic">Forskal</hi>. l.c. p. 12, and <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, 1, p. 379), they will eat carrion if it is still fresh and not decomposed; so that the eating of carrion could very properly be attributed to them in such passages as <reference osisRef="Job.39.30">Job 39:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.17">Pro 30:17</reference>, and Mat 24:28. But the bald-headedness mentioned in Mic 1:16 applies, not to the true eagle, but to the carrion-kite, which is reckoned, however, among the different species of eagles, as well as the bearded or golden vulture. The next in the list is <hi type="italic">peres</hi>, from <hi type="italic">paras</hi> = <hi type="italic">parash</hi> to break, <hi type="italic">ossifragus</hi>, i.e., wither the bearded or golden vulture, <hi type="italic">gypaetos barbatus</hi>, or more probably, as <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi> supposes, the <hi type="italic">sea-eagle</hi>, which may have been the species intended in the γρύψ = γρυπαίετος of the lxx and <hi type="italic">gryphus</hi> of the Vulgate, and to which the ancients seem sometimes to have applied the name <hi type="italic">ossifraga</hi> (<hi type="italic">Lucret</hi>. v. 1079). By the next, עזניּה, we are very probably to understand the <hi type="italic">bearded</hi> or <hi type="italic">golden vulture</hi>. For this word is no doubt connected with the Arabic word for beard, and therefore points to the golden vulture, which has a tuft of hair or feathers on the lower beak, and which might very well be associated with the eagles so far as the size is concerned, having wings that measure 10 feet from tip to tip. As it really belongs to the family of cultures, it forms a very fitting link of transition to the other species of vulture and falcon (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.14">Lev 11:14</reference>). דּאה (<hi type="italic">Deut</hi>. דּיּה, according to a change which is by no means rare when the <hi type="italic">aleph</hi> stands between two vowels: cf. דּואג in <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.8">1Sa 21:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9">1Sa 22:9</reference>, and דּויג in <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.18">1Sa 22:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.22">1Sa 22:22</reference>), from דּאה to fly, is either the <hi type="italic">kite</hi>, or the <hi type="italic">glede</hi>, which is very common in Palestine (<hi type="italic">v. Schubert, Reise</hi> iii. p. 120), and lives on carrion. It is a gregarious bird (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.34.15">Isa 34:15</reference>), which other birds of prey are not, and is used by many different tribes as food (<hi type="italic">Oedmann</hi>, iii. p. 120). The conjecture that the black glede-kite is meant, - a bird which is particularly common in the East, - and that the name is derived from דּאה to be dark, is overthrown by the use of the word למינהּ in Deuteronomy, which shows that דאה is intended to denote the whole genus. איּה, which is referred to in <reference osisRef="Job.28.7">Job 28:7</reference> as sharp-sighted, is either the falcon, several species of which are natives of Syria and Arabia, and which is noted for its keen sight and the rapidity of its flight, or according to the <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi>, <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>, etc., <hi type="italic">vultur</hi>, the true vulture (the lxx have Ἰκτίν, the kite, here, and γρύψ, the griffin, in Deut. and Job), of which there are three species in Palestine (<hi type="italic">Lynch</hi>, p. 229). In <reference osisRef="Deut.14.13">Deu 14:13</reference> הראה is also mentioned, from ראה to see. Judging from the name, it was a keen-sighted bird, either a falcon or another species of vulture (<hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>. <hi type="italic">ixion</hi>).
entries.d2ae8205bfe94faa1bacb2844b1dee973019691a: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.15">Lev 11:15</reference> <div eID="gen1286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1287" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Every raven after his kind,</hi>” i.e., the whole genus of ravens, with the rest of the raven-like birds, such as crows, jackdaws, and jays, which are all of them natives of Syria and Palestine. The omission of ו before את, which is found in several MSS and editions, is probably to be regarded as the true reading, as it is not wanting before any of the other names.
entries.483294e8120efc88f4849c731c57bba49aec39d4: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.16-Lev.11.19">Lev 11:16-19</reference> היּענה בּת, i.e., either daughter of screaming (<hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>), or daughter of greediness (<hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>, etc.), is used according to all the ancient versions for the ostrich, which is more frequently described as the dweller in the desert (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.21">Isa 13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.13">Isa 34:13</reference>, etc.), or as the mournful screamer (Mic 1:8; <reference osisRef="Job.30.29">Job 30:29</reference>), and is to be understood, not as denoting the female ostrich only, but as a noun of common gender denoting the ostrich generally. It does not devour carrion indeed, but it eats vegetable matter of the most various kinds, and swallows greedily stones, metals, and even glass. It is found in Arabia, and sometimes in Hauran and Belka (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi> and <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>), and has been used as food not only by the Struthiophagi of Ethiopia (<hi type="italic">Diod. Sic. </hi> 3, 27; <hi type="italic">Strabo</hi>, xvi. 772) and Numidia (<hi type="italic">Leo Afric</hi>. p. 766), but by some of the Arabs also (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, iii. p. 20; <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, p. 178), whilst others only eat the eggs, and make use of the fat in the preparation of food. תּחמס, according to <hi type="italic">Bochart, Gesenius,</hi> and others, is the male ostrich; but this is very improbable. According to the lxx, <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>., and others, it is the <hi type="italic">owl</hi> (<hi type="italic">Oedmann</hi>, iii. pp. 45ff.); but this is mentioned later under another name. According to <hi type="italic">Saad. Ar. Erp. </hi>it is the <hi type="italic">swallow</hi>; but this is called סיס in Jer 8:7. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes it to be the <hi type="italic">cuckoo</hi>, which is met with in Palestine (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, 1, p. 78), and derives the name from חמס, <hi type="italic">violenter egit</hi>, supposing it to be so called from the violence with which it is said to turn out or devour the eggs and young of other birds, for the purpose of laying its own eggs in the nest (<hi type="italic">Aristot. hist. an.</hi> 6, 7; 9, 29; <hi type="italic">Ael. nat. an.</hi> 6, 7). שׁחף is the λάρος, or <hi type="italic">slender gull</hi>, according to the lxx and <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> follows the Arabic, however, and supposes it to be a species of <hi type="italic">hawk</hi>, which is trained in Syria for hunting gazelles, hares, etc.; but this is certainly included in the genus נץ. נץ, from נצץ to fly, is the <hi type="italic">hawk</hi>, which soars very high, and spreads its wings towards the south (<reference osisRef="Job.39.26">Job 39:26</reference>). It stands in fact, as למינהוּ shows, for the hawk-tribe generally, probably the ἱέραξ, <hi type="italic">accipiter</hi>, of which the ancients enumerate many different species. כּוס, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.7">Psa 102:7</reference> as dwelling in ruins, is an <hi type="italic">owl</hi> according to the ancient versions, although they differ as to the kind. In <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> opinion it is either the <hi type="italic">screech-owl</hi>, which inhabits ruined buildings, walls, and clefts in the rock, and the flesh of which is said to be very agreeable, or the <hi type="italic">little screech-owl</hi>, which also lives in old buildings and walls, and raises a mournful cry at night, and the flesh of which is said to be savoury. שׁלך, according to the ancient versions an aquatic bird, and therefore more in place by the side of the heron, where it stands in Deuteronomy, is called by the lxx καταῤῥάκτης; in the <hi type="italic">Targ</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Syr</hi>. נוּנא שׁלי, <hi type="italic">extrahens pisces</hi>. It is not the <hi type="italic">gull</hi>, however (<hi type="italic">larus catarractes</hi>), which plunges with violence, for according to <hi type="italic">Oken</hi> this is only seen in the northern seas, but a species of <hi type="italic">pelican</hi>, to be found on the banks of the Nile and in the islands of the Red Sea, which swims well, and also dives, frequently dropping perpendicularly upon fishes in the water. The flesh has an oily taste, but it is eaten for all that. ינשׁוּף: from נשׁף to snort, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">Isa 34:11</reference>, dwelling in ruins, no doubt a species of <hi type="italic">owl</hi>; according to the Chaldee and Syriac, the <hi type="italic">uhu</hi>, which dwells in old ruined towers and castles upon the mountains, and cries <hi type="italic">uhupuhu</hi>. תּנשׁמת, which occurs again in <reference osisRef="Lev.11.30">Lev 11:30</reference> among the names of the lizards, is, according to <hi type="italic">Damiri</hi>, a bird resembling the <hi type="italic">uhu</hi>, but smaller. <hi type="italic">Jonathan</hi> calls it <hi type="italic">uthya</hi> = ὠτός, a <hi type="italic">night-owl</hi>. The primary meaning of the word נשׁם is essentially the same as that of נשׁף, to breathe or blow, so called because many of the owls have a mournful cry, and blow and snort in addition; though it cannot be decided whether the <hi type="italic">strix otus</hi> is intended, a bird by no means rare in Egypt, which utters a whistling blast, and rolls itself into a ball and then spreads itself out again, or the <hi type="italic">strix flammea</hi>, a native of Syria, which sometimes utters a mournful cry, and at other times snores like a sleeping man, and the flesh of which is said to be by no means unpleasant, or the hissing owl (<hi type="italic">strix stridula</hi>), which inhabits the ruins in Egypt and Syria, and is sometimes called <hi type="italic">massusu</hi>, at other times <hi type="italic">bane</hi>, a very voracious bird, which is said to fly in at open windows in the evening and kill children that are left unguarded, and which is very much dreaded in consequence. קאת, which also lived in desolate places (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">Isa 34:11</reference>; Zep 2:14), or in the desert itself (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.7">Psa 102:7</reference>), was not the <hi type="italic">katà</hi>, a species of partridge or heath-cock, which is found in Syria (Robinson, ii. p. 620), as this bird always flies in large flocks, and this is not in harmony with <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">Isa 34:11</reference> and Zep 2:14, but the <hi type="italic">pelican</hi> (πελεκάν, lxx), as all the ancient versions render it, which <hi type="italic">Ephraem</hi> (on Num 14:17) describes as a marsh-bird, very fond of its young, inhabiting desolate places, and uttering an incessant cry. It is the true pelican of the ancients (<hi type="italic">pelecanus graculus</hi>), the Hebrew name of which seems to have been derived from קוא to spit, from its habit of spitting out the fishes it has caught, and which is found in Palestine and the reedy marshes of Egypt (Robinson, Palestine). רחם, in Deut. רחמה, is κυκνός, the swan, according to the Septuagint; <hi type="italic">porphyrio</hi>, the fish-heron, according to the Vulgate; a marsh-bird therefore, possibly <hi type="italic">vultur percnopterus</hi> (<hi type="italic">Saad. Ar. Erp.</hi>), which is very common in Arabia, Palestine, and Syria, and was classed by the ancients among the different species of eagles (<hi type="italic">Plin. h. n. </hi> 10, 3), but which is said to resemble the vulture, and was also called ὀρειπέλαργος, the mountain-stork (<hi type="italic">Arist. h. an. </hi>9, 32). It is a stinking and disgusting bird, of the raven kind, with black pinions; but with this exception it is quite white. It is also bald-headed, and feeds on carrion and filth. But it is eaten notwithstanding by many of the Arabs (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt, Syr.</hi> p. 1046). It received its name of “<hi type="italic">tenderly loving</hi>” from the tenderness with which it watches over its young (<hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>, iii. pp. 56, 57). In this respect it resembles the stork, חסידה, <hi type="italic">avis pia</hi>, a bird of passage according to <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jer 8:7</reference>, which builds its nest upon the cypresses (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.17">Psa 104:17</reference>, cf. <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>, iii. pp. 85ff.). In the East the stork builds its nest not only upon high towers and the roofs of houses, but according to <hi type="italic">Kazwini</hi> and others mentioned by <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi> (iii. p. 60), upon lofty trees as well.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Oedmann</hi> (v. 58ff.), <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, and others follow the Greek translation of Leviticus and the Psalms, and the <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi> rendering of Leviticus, the Psalms, and Job, and suppose the reference to be to the ἐρωδιός, <hi type="italic">herodius</hi>, the heron: but the name <hi type="italic">chasidah</hi> points decidedly to the stork, which was generally regarded by the ancients as <hi type="italic">pietatis cultrix</hi> (<hi type="italic">Petron</hi>. 55, 6), whereas, with the exception of the somewhat indefinite passage in <hi type="italic">Aelian</hi> (<hi type="italic">Nat. an.</hi> 3, 23), καὶ τοὺς ἐρωδιοὺς ἀκούω ποιεῖν ταὐτόν (i.e., feed their young by spitting out their food) καὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας μέντοι, nothing is said about the parental affection of the heron. And the testimony of <hi type="italic">Bellonius</hi>, “<hi type="italic">Ciconiae quae aetate in Europa sunt, magna hyemis parte ut in Aegypto sic etiam circa Antiochiam et juxta Amanum montem degunt</hi>,” is a sufficient answer to <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> assertion, that according to Seetzen there are not storks in Mount Lebanon.</note> אנפה, according to the lxx and <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi> χαραδριός, a marsh-bird of the <hi type="italic">snipe</hi> kind, of which there are several species in Egypt (<hi type="italic">Hasselquist</hi>, p. 308). This is quite in accordance with the expression “after her kind,” which points to a numerous genus. The omission of ואת before האנפה, whereas it is found before the name of every other animal, is very striking; but as the name is preceded by the copulative <hi type="italic">vav</hi> in Deuteronomy, and stands for a particular bird, it may be accounted for either from a want of precision on the part of the author, or from an error of the copyist like the omission of the ו before את in Lev 11:15.<note placement="foot">On account of the omission of ואת <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> would connect האנפה as an adjective with החסידה, and explain אנף as derived from ענף <hi type="italic">frons</hi>, ענף <hi type="italic">frondens</hi>, and signifying bushy. The herons were called “the bushy <hi type="italic">chasidah</hi>,” he supposes, because they have a tuft of feathers at the back of their head, or long feathers hanging down from their neck, which are wanting in the other marsh-birds, such as the flamingo, crane, and ibis. But there is this important objection to the explanation, that the change of א for ע in such a word as ענף frons, which occurs as early as <reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">Lev 23:40</reference>, and has retained its ע even in the Aramaean dialects, is destitute of all probability. In addition to this, there is the improbability of the <hi type="italic">chasidah</hi> being restricted by <hi type="italic">anaphah</hi> to the different species of heron, with three of which the ancients were acquainted (<hi type="italic">Aristot. h. an. </hi>9, 2; <hi type="italic">Plin. h. n.</hi> 10, 60). If <hi type="italic">chasidah</hi> denoted the heron generally, or the white heron, the epithet <hi type="italic">anaphah</hi> would be superfluous. It would be necessary to assume, therefore, that <hi type="italic">chasidah</hi> denotes the whole tribe of marsh-birds, and that Moses simply intended to prohibit the heron or bushy marsh-bird. But either of these is very improbable: the former, because in every other passage of the Old Testament <hi type="italic">chasidah</hi> stands for one particular kind of bird; the latter, because Moses could hardly have excluded storks, ibises, and other marsh-birds that live on worms, from his prohibition. All that remains, therefore, is to separate <hi type="italic">ha</hi>-<hi type="italic">anaphah</hi> from the preceding word, as in Deuteronomy, and to understand it as denoting the plover (?) or heron, as there were several species of both. Which is intended, it is impossible to decide, as there is nothing certain to be gathered from either the ancient versions or the etymology. <hi type="italic">Bochart's</hi> reference of the word to a fierce bird, viz., a species of eagle, which the Arabs call <hi type="italic">Tammaj</hi>, is not raised into a probability by a comparison with the similarly sounding ἀνοπαῖα of Od. 1, 320, by which <hi type="italic">Aristarchus</hi> understands a kind of eagle.</note> דּוּכיפת: according to the lxx, <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>., and others, the <hi type="italic">lapwing</hi>, which is found in Syria, Arabia, and still more commonly in Egypt (<hi type="italic">Forsk, Russel, Sonnini</hi>), and is eaten in some places, as its flesh is said to be fat and savoury in autumn (<hi type="italic">Sonn</hi>. 1, 204). But it has a disagreeable smell, as it frequents marshy districts seeking worms and insects for food, and according to a common belief among the ancients, builds its nest of human dung. Lastly, העטלּף is the bat (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Isa 2:20</reference>), which the Arabs also classified among the birds.
entries.a7ac91d482872e710f93ea09205b970698e5dc39: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.20-Lev.11.23">Lev 11:20-23</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.14.19">Deu 14:19</reference>). To the birds there are appended flying animals of other kinds: “<hi type="italic">all swarms of fowl that go upon fours,</hi>” i.e., the smaller winged animals with four feet, which are called <hi type="italic">sherez</hi>, “swarms,” on account of their multitude. These were not to be eaten, as they were all abominations, with the exception of those “<hi type="italic">which have two shank-feet above their feet </hi>(i.e., springing feet) <hi type="italic">to leap with</hi>” (לא for לו as in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.8">Exo 21:8</reference>). Locusts are the animals referred to, four varieties being mentioned with their different species (“<hi type="italic">after his kind</hi>”); but these cannot be identified with exactness, as there is still a dearth of information as to the natural history of the oriental locust. It is well known that locusts were eaten by many of the nations of antiquity both in Asia and Africa, and even the ancient Greeks thought the <hi type="italic">Cicades</hi> very agreeable in flavour (<hi type="italic">Arist. h. an. </hi>5, 30). In Arabia they are sold in the market, sometimes strung upon cords, sometimes by measure; and they are also dried, and kept in bags for winter use. For the most part, however, it is only by the poorer classes that they are eaten, and many of the tribes of Arabia abhor them (Robinson, ii. p. 628); and those who use them as food do not eat all the species indiscriminately. They are generally cooked over hot coals, or on a plate, or in an oven, or stewed in butter, and eaten either with salt or with spice and vinegar, the head, wings, and feet being thrown away. They are also boiled in salt and water, and eaten with salt or butter. Another process is to dry them thoroughly, and then grind them into meal and make cakes of them. The Israelites were allowed to eat the <hi type="italic">arbeh</hi>, i.e., according to <reference osisRef="Exod.10.13">Exo 10:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.10.19">Exo 10:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Nah 3:17</reference>, etc., the flying migratory locust, <hi type="italic">gryllus migratorius</hi>, which still bears this name, according to <hi type="italic">Niebuhr</hi>, in Maskat and Bagdad, and is poetically designated in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.46">Psa 78:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.34">Psa 105:34</reference>, as חסיל, <hi type="italic">the devourer</hi>, and ילק, <hi type="italic">the eater-up;</hi> but <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> is mistaken in supposing that these names are applied to certain species of the <hi type="italic">arbeh</hi>. סלעם, according to the Chaldee, <hi type="italic">deglutivit</hi>, <hi type="italic">absorpsit</hi>, is unquestionably a larger and peculiarly voracious species of locust. This is all that can be inferred from the rashon of the Targums and Talmud, whilst the ἀττάκης and <hi type="italic">attacus</hi> of the lxx and Vulg. are altogether unexplained. חרגּל: according to the Arabic, a galloping, i.e., a hopping, not a flying species of locust. This is supported by the Samaritan, also by the lxx and <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>., ὀφιομάχης, <hi type="italic">ophiomachus</hi>. According to <hi type="italic">Hesychius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Suidas</hi>, it was a species of locust without wings, probably a very large kind; as it is stated in <hi type="italic">Mishnah</hi>, <hi type="italic">Shabb</hi>. vi. 10, that an egg of the <hi type="italic">chargol</hi> was sometimes suspended in the ear, as a remedy for earache. Among the different species of locusts in Mesopotamia, <hi type="italic">Niebuhr</hi> (Arab. p. 170) saw two of a very large size with springing feet, but without wings. חגב, a word of uncertain etymology, occurs in Num 13:33, where the spies are described as being like <hi type="italic">chagabim</hi> by the side of the inhabitants of the country, and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.13">2Ch 7:13</reference>, where the <hi type="italic">chagab</hi> devours the land. From these passages we may infer that it was a species of locust without wings, small but very numerous, probably the ἀττέλαβος, which is often mentioned along with the ἀκρίς, but as a distinct species, <hi type="italic">locustarum minima sine pennis</hi> (<hi type="italic">Plin. h. n.</hi> 29, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. 4, <hi type="italic">s</hi>. 29), or <hi type="italic">parva locusta modicis pennis reptans potius quam volitans semperque subsiliens</hi> (<hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> (on <reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Nah 3:17</reference>).<note placement="foot">In <reference osisRef="Deut.14.19">Deu 14:19</reference> the edible kinds of locusts are passed over, because it was not the intention of Moses to repeat every particular of the earlier laws in these addresses. But when <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> (on Lev. pp. 455 and 461) gives this explanation of the omission, that the eating of locusts is prohibited in Deuteronomy, and the Deuteronomist passes them over because in his more advanced age there was apparently no longer any necessity for the prohibition, this arbitrary interpretation is proved to be at variance with historical truth by the fact that locusts were eaten by John the Baptist, inasmuch as this proves at all events that a more advanced age had not given up the custom of eating locusts.</note>
entries.d20018072cc791a9b4cecb175dba9e469cf64f6c: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.24-Lev.11.26">Lev 11:24-26</reference> <div eID="gen1287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1288" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Lev.11.24-Lev.11.28">Lev 11:24-28</reference> there follow still further and more precise instructions, concerning defilement through contact with the carcases (i.e., the carrion) of the animals already mentioned. These instructions relate first of all (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.24">Lev 11:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.11.25">Lev 11:25</reference>) to aquatic and winged animals, which were not to be eaten because they were unclean (the expression “<hi type="italic">for these</hi>” in <reference osisRef="Lev.11.24">Lev 11:24</reference> relates to them); and then (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.26-Lev.11.28">Lev 11:26-28</reference>) to quadrupeds, both cattle that have not the hoof thoroughly divided and do not ruminate (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.26">Lev 11:26</reference>), and animals that go upon their hands, i.e., upon paws, and have no hoofs, such as cats, dogs, bears, etc.
entries.cf2b2260cb0306a394e48a9c51f924cba9099b8b: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.27-Lev.11.28">Lev 11:27-28</reference> <div eID="gen1288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1289" type="x-p"/> The same rule was applicable to all these animals: “<hi type="italic">whoever toucheth the carcase of them shall be unclean until the even,</hi>” i.e., for the rest of the day; he was then of course to wash himself. Whoever carried their carrion, viz., to take it away, was also unclean till the evening, and being still more deeply affected by the defilement, he was to wash his clothes as well.
entries.210efeb0e31a8ef93f0865e127ea02c7e2e94ce1: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.29-Lev.11.38">Lev 11:29-38</reference> <div eID="gen1289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1290" type="x-p"/> To these there are attached analogous instructions concerning defilement through contact with the smaller creeping animals (<hi type="italic">Sherez</hi>), which formed the fourth class of the animal kingdom; though the prohibition against eating these animals is not introduced till <reference osisRef="Lev.11.41">Lev 11:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.42">Lev 11:42</reference>, as none of these were usually eaten. <hi type="italic">Sherez</hi>, the swarm, refers to animals which swarm together in great numbers (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.1.21">Gen 1:21</reference>), and is synonymous with <hi type="italic">remes</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.7.14">Gen 7:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.7.21">Gen 7:21</reference>), “the creeping;” it denotes the smaller land animals which move without feet, or with feet that are hardly perceptible (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.1.24">Gen 1:24</reference>). Eight of the creeping animals are named, as defiling not only the men with whom they might come in contact, but any domestic utensils and food upon which they might fall; they were generally found in houses, therefore, or in the abodes of men. חלד is not the <hi type="italic">mole</hi> (according to <hi type="italic">Saad. Ar. Abys.</hi>, etc.), although the Arabs still call this <hi type="italic">chuld</hi>, but the <hi type="italic">weasel</hi> (lxx, <hi type="italic">Onk</hi>., etc.), which is common in Syria and Palestine, and is frequently mentioned by the Talmudists in the feminine form חוּלדה, as an animal which caught birds (<hi type="italic">Mishn. Cholin</hi> iii. 4), which would run over the wave-loaves with a sherez in its mouth (<hi type="italic">Mishn. Tohor</hi>. iv. 2), and which could drink water out of a vessel (<hi type="italic">Mishn. Para</hi> ix. 3). עכבּר is the <hi type="italic">mouse</hi> (according to the ancient versions and the Talmud), and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.5">1Sa 6:5</reference> the <hi type="italic">field-mouse</hi>, the scourge of the fields, not the jerboa, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes; for this animal lives in holes in the ground, is very shy, and does not frequent houses as is assumed to be the case with the animals mentioned here. צב is a kind of lizard, but whether the <hi type="italic">thav</hi> or <hi type="italic">dsabb</hi>, a harmless yellow lizard of 18 inches in length, which is described by <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, iii. pp. 436ff., also by <hi type="italic">Hasselquist</hi> under the name of <hi type="italic">lacerta Aegyptia</hi>, or the <hi type="italic">waral</hi>, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes, a large land lizard reaching as much as four feet in length, which is also met with in Palestine (Robinson, ii. 160) and is called <hi type="italic">el worran</hi> by <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, cannot be determined.
entries.939e3a0ed2ce4b34a02a023ad303e23fa8933bbf: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.39-Lev.11.45">Lev 11:39-45</reference> <div eID="gen1298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1299" type="x-p"/> Lastly, contact with edible animals, if they had not been slaughtered, but had died a natural death, and had become carrion in consequence, is also said to defile (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.11.39">Lev 11:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.40">Lev 11:40</reference> with <reference osisRef="Lev.11.24-Lev.11.28">Lev 11:24-28</reference>). This was the case, too, with the eating of the swarming land animals, whether they went upon the belly,<note placement="foot">The large ו in גּחון (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.42">Lev 11:42</reference>) shows that this <hi type="italic">vav</hi> is the middle letter of the Pentateuch.</note> as snakes and worms, or upon four feet, as rats, mice, weasels, etc., or upon many feet, like the insects (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.41-Lev.11.43">Lev 11:41-43</reference>). Lastly (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.44">Lev 11:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.45">Lev 11:45</reference>), the whole law is enforced by an appeal to the calling of the Israelites, as a holy nation, to be holy as Jehovah their God, who had brought them out of Egypt to be a God to them, was holy (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.7">Exo 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.45-Exod.29.46">Exo 29:45-46</reference>).
entries.b21a371fd2f3a4a70e3eb7eb829863bcda5acdf8: <reference osisRef="Lev.11.46-Lev.11.47">Lev 11:46-47</reference> <div eID="gen1299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1300" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lev.11.46">Lev 11:46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.47">Lev 11:47</reference> contain the concluding formula to the whole of this law. If we take a survey, in closing, of the animals that are enumerated as unclean and not suitable for food, we shall find that among the larger land animals they were chiefly beasts of prey, that seize upon other living creatures and devour them in their blood; among the water animals, all snake-like fishes and slimy shell-fish; among birds, the birds of prey, which watch for the life of other animals and kill them, the marsh-birds, which live on worms, carrion, and all kinds of impurities, and such mongrel creatures as the ostrich, which lives in the desert, and the bat, which flies about in the dark; and lastly, all the smaller animals, with the exception of a few graminivorous locusts, but more especially the snake-like lizards, - partly because they called to mind the old serpent, partly because they crawled in the dust, seeking their food in mire and filth, and suggested the thought of corruption by the slimy nature of their bodies. They comprised, in fact, all such animals as exhibited more or less the darker type of sin, death, and corruption; and it was on this ethical ground alone, and not for all kinds of sanitary reasons, or even from political motives, that the nation of Israel, which was called to sanctification, was forbidden to eat them. It is true there are several animals mentioned as unclean, e.g., the ass, the camel, and others, in which we can no longer recognise this type. But we must bear in mind, that the distinction between clean animals and unclean goes back to the very earliest times (<reference osisRef="Gen.7.2-Gen.7.3">Gen 7:2-3</reference>), and that in relation to the large land animals, as well as to the fishes, the Mosaic law followed the marks laid down by tradition, which took its rise in the primeval age, whose childlike mind, acute perception, and deep intuitive insight into nature generally, discerned more truly and essentially the real nature of the animal creation than we shall ever be able to do, with thoughts and perceptions disturbed as ours are by the influences of unnatural and ungodly culture.<note placement="foot">“In its direct and deep insight into the entire <hi type="italic">nexus</hi> of the physical, psychical, and spiritual world, into the secret correspondences of the <hi type="italic">cosmos</hi> and <hi type="italic">nomos</hi>, this sense for nature anticipated discoveries which we shall never make with our ways of thinking, but which a purified humanity, when looking back from the new earth, will fully understand, and will no longer only 'see through a glass darkly.'” - <hi type="italic">Leyrer, Herzog's</hi> Cycl.</note> Laws of Purification - Leviticus 12-15 <div eID="gen1300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1301" type="x-p"/> The laws concerning defilement through eating unclean animals, or through contact with those that had died a natural death, are followed by rules relating to defilements proceeding from the human body, in consequence of which persons contaminated by them were excluded for a longer or shorter period from the fellowship of the sanctuary, and sometimes even from intercourse with their fellow-countrymen, and which had to be removed by washing, by significant lustrations, and by expiatory sacrifices. They comprised the uncleanness of a woman in consequence of child-bearing (<reference osisRef="Lev.12.1-Lev.12.8">Lev 12:1-8</reference>), leprosy (ch. 13 and 14), and both natural and diseased secretions from the sexual organs of either male or female (<hi type="italic">emissio seminis</hi> and gonorrhaea, also menses and flux: ch. 15); and to these there is added in Num 19:11-22, defilement proceeding from a human corpse. Involuntary emission defiled the man; voluntary emission, in sexual intercourse, both the man and the woman and any clothes upon which it might come, for an entire day, and this defilement was to be removed in the evening by bathing the body, and by washing the clothes, etc. (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.16-Lev.15.18">Lev 15:16-18</reference>). Secretions from the sexual organs, whether of a normal kind, such as the menses and those connected with child-birth, or the result of disease, rendered not only the persons affected with them unclean, but even their couches and seats, and any persons who might sit down upon them; and this uncleanness was even communicated to persons who touched those who were diseased, or to anything with which they had come in contact (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.3-Lev.15.12">Lev 15:3-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.19-Lev.15.27">Lev 15:19-27</reference>). In the case of the menses, the uncleanness lasted seven days (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.19">Lev 15:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.24">Lev 15:24</reference>); in that of child-birth, either seven or fourteen days, and then still further thirty-three or sixty-six, according to circumstances (<reference osisRef="Lev.12.2">Lev 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.12.4-Lev.12.5">Lev 12:4-5</reference>); and in that of a diseased flux, as long as the disease itself lasted, and seven days afterwards (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.13">Lev 15:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.28">Lev 15:28</reference>); but the uncleanness communicated to others only lasted till the evening. In all these cases the purification consisted in the bathing of the body and washing of the clothes and other objects. But if the uncleanness lasted more than seven days, on the day after the purification with water a sin-offering and a burnt-offering were to be offered, that the priest might pronounce the person clean, or receive him once more into the fellowship of the holy God (<reference osisRef="Lev.12.6">Lev 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.12.8">Lev 12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.15.14-Lev.15.15">Lev 15:14-15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.29-Lev.15.30">Lev 15:29-30</reference>). Leprosy made those who were affected with it so unclean, that they were excluded from all intercourse with the clean (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45-Lev.13.46">Lev 13:45-46</reference>): and on their recovery they were to be cleansed by a solemn lustration, and received again with sacrifices into the congregation of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.1-Lev.14.32">Lev 14:1-32</reference>). There are no express instructions as to the communicability of leprosy; but this is implied in the separation of the leper from the clean (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45-Lev.13.46">Lev 13:45-46</reference>), as well as from the fact that a house affected by the leprosy rendered all who entered it, or slept in it, unclean (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.46-Lev.14.47">Lev 14:46-47</reference>). The defilement caused by a death was apparently greater still. Not only the corpse of a person who had died a natural death, as well as of one who had been killed by violence, but a dead body or grave defiled, for a period of seven days, both those who touched them, and (in the case of the corpse) the house in which the man had died, all the persons who were in it or might enter it, and all the open vessels that were there (Num 19:11, Num 19:14-16). Uncleanness of this kind could only be removed by sprinkling water prepared from running water and the ashes of a sin-offering (Num 19:12, Num 19:17.), and would even spread from the persons defiled to persons and things with which they came in contact, so as to render them unclean till the evening (Num 19:22); whereas the defilement caused by contact with a dead animal lasted only a day, and then, like every other kind of uncleanness that only lasted till the evening, could be removed by bathing the persons or washing the things (Lev 11:25.). <div eID="gen1301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1302" type="x-p"/> But whilst, according to this, generation and birth as well as death were affected with uncleanness; generation and death, the coming into being and the going out of being, were not defiling in themselves, or regarded as the two poles which bound, determine, and enclose the finite existence, so as to warrant us in tracing the principle which lay at the foundation of the laws of purification, as <hi type="italic">Bähr</hi> supposes, “to the antithesis between the infinite and the finite being, which falls into the sphere of the sinful when regarded ethically as the opposite to the absolutely holy.” Finite existence was created by God, quite as much as the corporeality of man; and both came forth from His hand pure and good. Moreover it is not begetting, giving birth, and dying, that are said to defile; but the secretions connected with generation and child-bearing, and the corpses of those who had died. In the decomposition which follows death, the effect of sin, of which death is the wages, is made manifest in the body. Decomposition, as the embodiment of the unholy nature of sin, is uncleanness κατ ̓ ἐξοχξήν; and this the Israelite, who was called to sanctification in fellowship with God, was to avoid and abhor. Hence the human corpse produced the greatest amount of defilement; so great, in fact, that to remove it a sprinkling water was necessary, which had been strengthened by the ashes of a sin-offering into a kind of sacred alkali. Next to the corpse, there came on the one hand <hi type="italic">leprosy</hi>, that bodily image of death which produced all the symptoms of decomposition even in the living body, and on the other hand the offensive secretions from the organs of generation, which resemble the putrid secretions that are the signs in the corpse of the internal dissolution of the bodily organs and the commencement of decomposition. From the fact that the impurities, for which special rites of purification were enjoined, are restricted to these three forms of manifestation in the human body, it is very evident that the laws of purification laid down in the O.T. were not regulations for the promotion of cleanliness or of good morals and decency, that is to say, were not police regulations for the protection of the life of the body from contagious diseases and other things injurious to health; but that their simple object was “to impress upon the mind a deep horror of everything that is and is called death in the creature, and thereby to foster an utter abhorrence of everything that is or is called sin, and also, to the constant humiliation of fallen man, to remind him in all the leading processes of the natural life-generation, birth, eating, disease, death - how everything, even his own bodily nature, lies under the curse of sin (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.14-Gen.3.19">Gen 3:14-19</reference>), that so the law might become a 'schoolmaster to bring unto Christ,' and awaken and sustain the longing for a Redeemer from the curse which had fallen upon his body also (see <reference osisRef="Gal.3.24">Gal 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Rom 7:24</reference>; Rom 8:19.; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Phi 3:21</reference>).” <hi type="italic">Leyrer</hi>.  <chapter eID="Lev.11"/> <div eID="gen1302" type="x-p"/>
